summary: A reply by Tom O'Sullivan to RFC 328. He agrees with dropping the minimum Telnet implementation in favor of one standard protocol. He argues that the Data Types and Hide Your Input signals should stay, since other codes are needed for devices like plotters and numerically controlled machines.

eli5.summary: Someone suggested removing some buttons from a remote-control. This person agrees about one, but says two buttons are still needed because some special gadgets use them.

subtitle: Arguments for keeping data type codes and password masking in Telnet.

tldr.problem: A proposal suggested simplifying Telnet by dropping the Data Types feature and the Hide Your Input feature. Some argue this would remove important capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC supports keeping both features: Data Types allow switches to special 8-bit codes needed by attached devices like plotters and machine tools; Hide Your Input lets password entry be masked.
tldr.outcome: Both features provide necessary support for specialized hardware and security, and can be improved with return codes and protocol enhancements.

today: RFC 340 comments on Telnet protocol design from May 1972 and is marked Unknown status. Modern Telnet does support both data types and password masking, and the arguments made here proved influential in protocol design decisions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC is a response to RFC 328, which proposed simplifying Telnet. Tom O'Sullivan agrees with the general direction but argues for keeping two features: Data Types and Hide Your Input (password masking). Removing these features would lose capabilities needed by specialized equipment and security-sensitive applications.
sections.eli5: In Telnet discussions, someone suggested removing two optional features. This person says those two features are still useful.

sections.title: Data Types
sections.content: Data Types allow Telnet to switch out of ASCII mode to handle arbitrary 8-bit codes. This is essential for terminals with attached specialized equipment. Examples include Calcomp plotters, numerically controlled machines, and sensor experiments. Each non-ASCII mode should provide a return code to ASCII. Data Types serve real use cases on the ARPANET.
sections.eli5: Some terminals have special gadgets plugged in (like a drawing machine or a drill controller) that use 8-bit codes the ASCII alphabet does not have. Telnet needs to handle this, and each gadget mode should have a way to get back to normal letters.

sections.title: Hide Your Input
sections.content:
Hide Your Input (password masking) masks characters as they are entered, so passwords and access keys do not appear on the console. With more network database systems coming online and requiring passwords, this feature becomes more important, not less.

The concern that it is hard to select the masking length can be solved by letting the server program specify how many characters to mask, with a reasonable default. Passwords and secrets are critical to network security, so this feature should stay.
sections.eli5: When you type a password, you want it hidden so nobody watching can see it. Network databases will need this more and more, so the feature is worth improving, not removing.

references.text: Crocker, D., "Telnet Protocol Specification", RFC 328, April 1972.
